title: UAE motorists to pay more as petrol prices rise again for June - DailyNews
summary:
The UAE has announced higher fuel prices for June 2026, with motorists set to pay more at the pump from June 1 as petrol prices continue their upward trend.

Super 98 petrol will cost Dhs3.95 per litre, up from Dhs3.66 in May, while Special 95 will rise to Dhs3.83 from Dhs3.55. E-Plus 91 will increase to Dhs3.76 from Dhs3.48.

Diesel, however, will fall to Dhs4.33 per litre, down from Dhs4.69 in May.

The latest revision marks the third consecutive monthly increase in petrol prices, reflecting broader movements in global oil markets.

For motorists, the latest increases will place added pressure on household budgets, with fuel remaining a regular monthly expense for many families. Even relatively small monthly price increases can have a noticeable impact on overall transport costs, particularly for daily commuters.

Super 98 has risen sharply this year, climbing from Dhs2.45 per litre in February — the lowest level recorded in 2026 so far — to Dhs3.95 in June.

The price trajectory has accelerated in recent months. Super 98 stood at Dhs2.53 in January before dipping to Dhs2.45 in February. It then rose to Dhs2.59 in March, jumped to Dhs3.39 in April, climbed again to Dhs3.66 in May and has now reached Dhs3.95 for June.

Diesel prices, by contrast, have eased this month, offering some relief to commercial operators and logistics firms.

The UAE has linked domestic fuel prices to average global oil prices since August 2015, when the government deregulated the sector and removed subsidies, exposing local pump prices to international market fluctuations.Gulf Business

title: Eleven dead as recovery efforts resume in Washington chemical tank rupture - DailyNews
summary:
Search crews are expected to navigate treacherous circumstances as they continue efforts to recover nine people, who are presumed dead, a day after a deadly chemical tank rupture at a paper plant in Washington state.

At least two were confirmed dead and another eight people were injured after a 900,000-gallon tank containing hazardous chemicals ruptured Tuesday morning at the Nippon Dynawave Packaging Co. facility in Longview. Officials said spillage from the tank sent contamination into the Columbia River, considered the lifeblood of the Pacific Northwest.

Officials originally said about 90,000 gallons of material could still be inside the damaged tank, but a subsequent inspection determined the amount to be roughly 25,000 gallons. That remaining liquid is believed to be on the opposite side of the tank from the leak, which is releasing material at a slower rate than on Tuesday, officials said. The tank contained a mixture called white liquor, which is used in paper-making processes and can cause second- and third-degree burns when it comes into contact with skin. Inhaling concentrated vapor around the liquid can also be dangerous, though it primarily acts as an irritant when in the air.

At least two were confirmed dead and another eight people were injured after a 900,000-gallon tank containing hazardous chemicals ruptured Tuesday morning at the Nippon Dynawave Packaging Co. facility in Longview. Officials said spillage from the tank sent contamination into the Columbia River, considered the lifeblood of the Pacific Northwest.

That remaining liquid is believed to be on the opposite side of the tank from the leak, which is releasing material at a slower rate than on Tuesday, officials said. title: Trump says Iran agrees to no nuclear weapons - DailyNews
summary:
US President Donald Trump said he had secured guarantees from Iran that it would not develop nuclear weapons, as reports emerged he had sent a tougher peace proposal back to Tehran.

Any tweaks to the proposal could prolong even further an agreement to formally end the Middle East war and open the Strait of Hormuz maritime route after weeks of efforts to secure a deal despite fractious rhetoric and the occasional flare up of armed conflict.

title: Israel captures strategic Crusader-built castle as incursion into southern Lebanon deepens - DailyNews
summary:
The Israeli military has captured the Crasader-era Beaufort Castle in southern Lebanon, a site it hasn’t held for 26 years, as it expands its incursion deeper into its neighbor’s territory.

The capture of the castle, near the city of Nabatiyeh and roughly 9 miles (14.5 kilometers) from the Israeli border, comes after days of fierce fighting in the area. “The operation is focused on establishing operational control of the Beaufort Ridge and the Wadi al-Saluki area,” the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) statement said Sunday, adding that it sought to dismantle Hezbollah infrastructure in both areas. The castle, which was built by the Crusaders on a high cliff overlooking the Litani River some 900 years ago, has long been considered a strategic site in southern Lebanon and has been occupied by Israeli forces during previous conflicts.

“The operation began several days ago, during which a significant number of IDF ground soldiers commenced offensive operations aimed at expanding the Forward Defense Line,” the IDF said. “From Beaufort Ridge, Hezbollah terrorists managed military and combat activities and carried out numerous attacks,” it said.

On Saturday, the Lebanese state news agency NNA reported Israeli air raids and “intense bombardment” in the area surrounding the castle. Hezbollah also claimed to have destroyed an Israeli tank near the castle. (CNN)

title: Sri Lankan-origin Nishan Velupillay named in Australia’s 2026 FIFA World Cup squad - DailyNews
summary:
Melbourne Victory’s 24 year old winger Nishan Velupillay has been selected for Australia’s final 26 man squad for the 2026 FIFA World Cup in North America.

Born to a Malaysian father of Sri Lankan Tamil descent and an Anglo-Indian mother, Velupillay’s inclusion marks a historic milestone for football players with Sri Lankan heritage.

After an impressive qualification campaign, which included scoring on his international debut against China, he joins a heavily refreshed Socceroos squad featuring 17 tournament debutants under coach Tony Popovic.

title: Sri Lanka win 2 Gold, 2 Silver, 4 Bronze medals - DailyNews
summary:
Sri Lanka’s promising middle distance athlete Tharushi Abhisheka (Podi Tharushi) once again came to the highlight when she clinched her second medal winning bronze in 800m women’s final at the final day of the Asian Under 20 Athletic Championship held in Hong Kong China yesterday. Tharushi is the only Sri Lankan athlete to win two individual medals in this meet.

Tharushi earlier won 1500 gold medal on the first day and bagged her second medal in 800m final yesterday with her personal best of 2.07.10  seconds to finish third. Japanese athlete Hanon Sasaki finished first with 2.05.44 seconds to win the gold while Chinese athlete Yue Deng finished second with a timing of 2.05.70 seconds to win the silver medal.

Meanwhile Nethsara Dineth  Liyanage (Akuramboda MV) won the silver medal in the men’s 800m final  yesterday. Venkatram Reddy of India won the gold with a clear lead clocking 1.48.27 seconds while Nethsara Dineth (1.49.22 secs) secured silver after a close fight with third placed Japanese athlete Atsuki Watanabe  (1.49.29 secs).

Sri Lanka’s 4x400m men’s relay team couldn’t make a podium finish ending fourth place yesterday.

Nethsara Dineth Liyanage

Ransini wins 200m gold

Earlier in the day three promising Lankan athlete Ransini Perera from Dharmapala Vidyalaya Pannipitiya created history winning the women’s 200m gold with 24.07 seconds. This is after Susanthika Jayasinghe won 200m gold medal for Sri Lanka 22 years ago during Asian Junior Championship in 1994 Ransini has won the gold for Sri Lanka.

Tharusha Mendis (Lyceum International Wattala) also won the silver medal in men’s high jump with a leap of 2.14 m while Sri Lanka 400m  mixed relay team won the bronze with a time of 3.38.66 seconds. Sri Lanka’s 4x400m mixed relay team, which finished fourth, was promoted to the bronze medal position after India was disqualified. The team comprised Sadew  Rajakaruna, Omel Shashintha Silva, Warsha Devmini, and Ronalee Peiris.

Sadew Rajakaruna  came back strongly to win the bronze with 21.13 seconds in 200m final

while Omel Shashintha was placed fourth in this same event with 21.21 seconds .

Meanwhile Tehara Ravishka placed 4th and Shasindu Hansana placed 6th in men’s Triple Jump finals while  Risansa Hirupama was placed 5th in women’s 200m final.

Twenty two Lankan athletes took part at this meet and they won 2 gold, 2 silver and 4 bronze medals.

Lankan medals medal winners at Asian U 20 Athletic Champiinship:

Tharushi Abhisheka – 1500m gold and 800m bronze. Ransini Perera –  200m gold. Mihansa Abeyratne  –  women’s high jump bronze. Tharusha Mendis – Men’s High Jump silver. Nethsara Dineth Liyanage – Men’s 800m silver. Sadew Rajakaruna – Men’s 200m bronze. Mixed 400m relay team (bronze) – Sadew  Rajakaruna,  Omel Shashintha Silva, Warsha Devmini, and Ronalee Peiris.

title: Devapathiraja U-19 Girls Div. One Champs - DailyNews
summary:
Devapathiraja College Rathgama emerged champions of the Under 19 Girl’s Division One Inter – Schools Cricket tournament conducted by Sri Lanka Schools Cricket Association and sponsored by Sri Lanka Cricket.

Devapathiraja College Rathgama beat Anula College Nugegoda in the final played at Wickramashila National School Giriulla on Thursday.

14 teams participated in this tournament. Shashini Gimhani of Devapathiraja College Rathgama did not play in this final as she is a member of Sri Lanka Women’s National squad.

Yesali Jithara of Anula College Nugegoda was adjudged the Player of the Final. Sanjana Kavindi of Devapathiraja College Rathgama was adjudged the Best Batter. Shehara Induwari of Devapathiraja College Rathgama was adjudged the Best Bowler.

Devapathiraja College Rathgama entered the final for the 10th time in the girl’s tournament and emerged champion for the eighth time.

title: Abhiru, Jessica clinch Open TT titles - DailyNews
summary:
Abhiru Perera of Killerspin TT Academy and Jessica Venya of Holy Cross College Gampaha emerged open men’s and women’s champions in the Sri Lanka Future Stars Table Tennis Championship conducted by Sportplus SC at Gateway College Indoor Stadium Colombo over the weekend.

Abhiru made two straight sets win (11-4 11-8)  over K.D.Chrish of Loyala College Bopitiya to win the men’s title at the final while Jessica defeated Minuli Hettiarachchi of Horizon International School Malabe with two sets (11-5,11-5) to win the women’s title.

Meanwhile two Gateway International school paddlers Aman Pasha and Senaya Amarathunga clinched the boys and girls under 17 titles. Aman made hard-fought three setter win (11-3,7-11,11-6)  over Pasas Wijekoon of Dharmaraja College.

Aman Pasha also came to the highlight  winning his second title as he clinched the  boys under 15 title after three setter game over Tharusha Wanniarachchi of Carey College Colombo.

In the Girls’ Under 17 final Senaya defeated her school mate Lakshi Gunasekara  (11-3,11-6).

The under 15 girls’ final was won by  Siyansa de Silva of Horizon International Malabe defeating Thesara Seymindee of Sirimavo Bandaranaike Vidyalaya Colombo (9-11,11-8,11-4).

The tournament gave good expourse for non ranking players to showcase their talent.

title: Lankan Rowers ready for Beach Sprint challenge in Thailand - DailyNews
summary:
Sri Lanka’s Beach Sprint Rowing team left for Thailand aiming to create history at the Asian Rowing Beach Sprint Championships 2026, which will be held at Jomtien Beach in Pattaya, Chonburi, from June 4 to 7.

The four-member squad will first take part in the Youth Athlete Development Training Camp from May 30 to June 3 before testing themselves against some of Asia’s top rowing nations in one of the sport’s fastest-growing disciplines.

The championship is expected to provide a major platform for Sri Lanka’s emerging coastal rowers as they seek to make their mark on the international stage.

The Sri Lankan delegation consists of experienced rower Major Maheshi Liyanage of the Sri Lanka Army, promising youngsters Denver Deheragoda of S. Thomas’ College, Mount Lavinia, and Vethmi Weeraratne of Visakha Vidyalaya, Colombo, along with coach Mangala Alagiyawanna.

The tour carries special significance for Sri Lankan rowing. Liyanage is set to become the first Sri Lankan woman to represent the country at an international Beach Rowing Championship in the Senior Women’s Single Scull category, opening a new chapter for women’s rowing in Sri Lanka.

Meanwhile, Weeraratne will also enter the record books as the first athlete from Visakha Vidyalaya to represent Sri Lanka at an international rowing championship, highlighting the growing reach of the sport among school athletes.

Liyanage will compete in the Senior Women’s Single Scull (CW1x) event. Deheragoda will take part in the Under-19 Men’s Single Scull (CM1x) and the Mixed Double Scull (CMix2x), while Weeraratne will contest the Under-19 Women’s Single Scull (CW1x) and the Mixed Double Scull (CMix2x).

Beach Sprint Rowing has rapidly gained popularity around the world due to its fast-paced and exciting format. Unlike traditional rowing, the event combines a sprint run on the beach, a dash into open water, buoy turns and a high-speed race back to shore, demanding both endurance and explosive power.

Sri Lanka’s participation was made possible through an invitation from the Rowing and Canoeing Association of Thailand (RCAT), with approval granted by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports of Sri Lanka.

Officials believe the championship will provide invaluable international exposure for the young Sri Lankan athletes while helping accelerate the development of coastal rowing and beach sprint rowing in the country.

With history on the line and a new generation of rowers eager to prove themselves, the Sri Lankan team will be hoping to ride the wave of opportunity and return home with performances that inspire the future of the sport.

The Asian Rowing Beach Sprint Championships are organised by the Rowing and Canoeing Association of Thailand under Asian rowing competition regulations and are expected to attract leading competitors from across the continent.

title: Royal end long wait by clinching Under-20 hockey title - DailyNews
summary:
Royal College Colombo created history when they emerged unbeaten champions of the All Island Under-20 Hockey Tournament after beating defending champions St. Thomas’ College, Matale in a dramatic sudden-death penalty shootout at the Rajarata University Grounds in Mihintale last week.

The thrilling final ended one all at full time before both teams remained locked at 4-4 in the regular penalty shootout. The contest then moved into sudden death, where Royal goalkeeper Stefan Anthonypillai produced a match-winning save and Rumal Jayasinghe converted the decisive stroke to hand Royal their first-ever Under-20 national hockey title since the tournament began in 2014.

Royal fought back strongly after trailing in the final and found a crucial equaliser just five minutes before the final whistle to keep their championship dream alive.

Goalkeeper Stefan Anthonypillai emerged as one of the heroes of the tournament. His  utstanding save diving to his right in the sudden-death shootout sealed the title and capped a remarkable week in which he guarded the Royal goal with confidence and consistency throughout  the seven matches. His performances earned him the award for the Best Goalkeeper of the Tournament.

Another key figure in Royal’s historic campaign was centre forward Savain Karunasiri. The talented striker scored important goals throughout the tournament, including crucial strikes in both the semi-final and final, proving to be a constant threat to opposing defences.

Royal’s journey to the title was far from easy. The Colombo school showed impressive consistency from the opening match despite having to adapt to an uneven grassy surface that was not ideal for fast-paced modern hockey.

They began by defeating Christ Church College, Matale 2-0 before edging traditional rivals St. Thomas’ College, Mount Lavinia 1-0. Victories over Kingswood College, Kandy by 2-0 and Maris Stella College, Negombo by 2-1 completed a flawless group-stage campaign.

The Reid Avenue boys then continued their winning run in the knockout stages. They defeated highly-rated Dharmadutha College, Badulla 2-0 in the quarter-final before overcoming a strong challenge from St. Joseph Vaz College, Wennappuwa with a hard-fought 1-0 victory in the semi-final.

Meanwhile, defending champions St. Thomas’ College, Matale reached the final after defeating Trinity College, Kandy 3-1 in the other semi-final. St. Joseph Vaz later secured third place with a 1-0 win over Trinity.

Behind Royal’s success was head coach Damith Panditharatne, whose long-term development programme finally delivered the ultimate reward. The former Sri Lanka and Air Force player, who previously coached Sri Lanka Police, has guided Royal since 2022 with strong support from the Royal College Hockey Club and former players.

The title also ended a long wait for national success. Royal had finished runners-up in the same tournament last year in Matale and had not won a national Under-20 hockey championship since capturing the National Schools Games title in 2017.

Adding further pride to their achievement, Royal were also named the Most Disciplined Team of the Tournament, highlighting the team’s excellent conduct both on and off the field.

title: Gary Kirsten conducts programme to educate school cricket coaches - DailyNews
summary:
Gary Kirsten the National Head coach  of Sri Lanka mens cricket  team emphasized the importance of creating a friendly and supportive environment for children while teaching cricketing skills at the special programme aimed at educating and developing school cricket coaches across the country.

Sri Lanka Cricket (SLC), under the direction of the Cricket Transformation Committee, has launched this  special programme at High Performance Center last Monday. with the participation of 74 coaches representing Division 1 and Division 2 schools.

Head Coach of the Sri Lanka Men’s Team Gary Kirsten conducted a two-hour session for the participating coaches, sharing insights into modern coaching methods and highlighting key areas coaches should focus on to nurture talented young cricketers.

Kirsten emphasized the importance of creating a friendly and supportive environment for children while teaching cricketing skills. He also noted that coaches must continuously improve their own skill levels to help develop successful players.

He encouraged school coaches to focus on producing quality cricketers rather than concentrating solely on winning matches.

Joining Kirsten at the programme were Ryan van Niekerk, National Bowling Coach, and Jordan Gregory, National Fielding and Spin Bowling Coach, who also shared their expertise and experiences with the coaches.

Sidath Wettimuny, Chairman of the Cricket Committee of Sri Lanka Cricket and a member of the Cricket Transformation Committee, delivered the introductory speech.

The programme also featured an interactive question-and-answer session, allowing participants to engage directly with Gary Kirsten and further enhance their knowledge.

title: Visakha divers reign supreme - DailyNews
summary:
Visakha Vidyalaya emerged as the overall  girls’ champions  at the 18th Sri Lanka Novices Diving Championships 2026, sponsored by MILO and held at the Sugathadasa Aquatic Sports Complex in Colombo recently.

Visakha topped the girls’ standings with 74 points, ahead of St. Bridget’s Convent with 68 points, as the country’s young diving stars showcased their talent across all age groups.

Visakha’s success was built on strong performances from the senior categories down to the junior divisions. In the Under-20 girls’ 1m Springboard event, Dinagi Gamage of Visakha Vidyalaya claimed the gold medal with 62.95 points. In the Under-18 category, Visakha swept the podium as Vihansa Bopagoda won gold with 60.50 points, Saheli Kulasekara secured silver with 56.15 points and Pamali Peeligama took bronze with 51.80 points.

The Under-16 girls’ competition was closely contested. Imandi Fernando of St. Bridget’s Convent won gold with 62.35 points in the 1m Springboard event, narrowly edging teammate Michella Gerald, who scored 62.25 points. Visakha’s Thesani Liyanage finished third with 62.00 points, while Miheli Liyanage was fourth.

In the Under-14 1m Springboard event, Chiranya Rodrigo of Visakha Vidyalaya delivered an impressive display to take gold with 97.45 points. Yaara Gunaratne of St. Bridget’s Convent won silver with 90.20 points, while Sahasya Mapitigama of Bishop’s College earned bronze with 74.65 points.

The Under-12 title went to Thinaya Ranasinghe of St. Bridget’s Convent with 98.80 points. Her teammate Giana Gunarathne secured silver with 88.35 points, while Chenuli Rajapaksha of Visakha Vidyalaya finished third with 80.75 points.

In the youngest Under-10 division, Oshini Chandraratne of Musaeus College captured the gold medal with 85.65 points. Shaheli Arya Ariyarattne of Visakha Vidyalaya claimed silver with 80.70 points, while Amaliya Nelson of Bishop’s College settled for bronze with 79.58 points.

The 3m Springboard events also produced several outstanding performances. Chiranya Rodrigo once again stole the spotlight by winning the Under-14 title with a championship-best score of 100.25 points. Yaara Gunarattne finished second with 90.55 points.

In the Under-16 3m Springboard event, Michelle Gerald of St. Bridget’s Convent secured gold with 72.35 points. The Under-12 title went to Tinaya Ranasinghe of St. Bridget’s Convent with 85.65 points, while Shenaya Karunarathne of Bishop’s College and Chenuli Rajapaksha of Visakha Vidyalaya completed the podium places.

Oshini Chandraratne continued her excellent form by winning the Under-10 3m Springboard event with 79.65 points, ahead of Tivya Jayamaha of Bishop’s College.

The overall girls’ standings saw Visakha Vidyalaya finish first with 74 points, followed by St. Bridget’s Convent on 68 points, Bishop’s College on 24 points and Musaeus College on 20 points.

title: Asian Athletics mourns death of Prema Pinnawala - DailyNews
summary:
General  Dahlan Al Hamad the President of Asian Athletics and Vice President of World Athletics in a  special message regarding the passing away of former Sri Lanka Athletic Secretary  Prema Pinnawala said that  It is with deep sadness and a heavy heart that I learnt of the passing  away of my dear friend, Prema Pinnawala of Sri Lanka.

He said that Prema dedicated more than five decades of his life to the service and development of athletics and the Olympic Movement not only in Sri Lanka but across Asia. His remarkable journey in sports administration, his wisdom, humility and commitment to athletics earned him the respect and admiration of all who had the privilege to work with him.

Personally, I have lost not only a colleague but one of my closest and dearest friends in athletics. Prema stood beside me through countless moments in Asian Athletics and became someone I trusted deeply and depended upon greatly. He was more than a respected administrator and leader, he was like a brother and a true right hand man whose loyalty, wisdom and sincerity never failed. The memories I shared over the years with him will always remain close to my heart.

On behalf of Asian Athletics Council and personally  I wish to express our heartfelt condolences to his wife, his daughters and the entire Sri Lankan Athletics and sports family The Asian Athletics family mourns the loss of a true gentleman, a respected leader and a dear friend. His lifelong dedication to athletics will always be remembered and cherished by all of us. May Almighty God grant him eternal peace and give strength and comfort to his family and loved ones.

title: The state of State schools - DailyNews
summary:
Sri Lanka has more than 10,000 state schools now. Schools, teachers, teaching, and schoolchildren have long been the subject of public discussion in the country. Over the past several decades, successive governments have introduced various changes to the education system. What truly matters, however, is what is actually happening inside state schools and the impact these institutions have on society at large. This is an area worthy of close examination.

The State-run education system comprises more than 10,155 Government schools. The system provides free education to children between the ages of five and fourteen. These schools fall into two main administrative categories: National Schools, which are centrally managed by the Ministry of Education, and Provincial Schools, which are administered by Provincial Councils.

At present, there are 373 National Schools in the country. Funded by the central government, they are generally well-resourced, highly competitive, and predominantly located in major urban centres such as Colombo and Kandy.

In addition, there are 9,782 Provincial Schools. Managed by Provincial Councils, they account for the vast majority of schools in the country and provide foundational education to students in communities across Sri Lanka.

The private schools, which is 104 in in number, is not the focus of this discussion. The private education sector is a broad subject that warrants separate consideration due to the numerous pressing issues associated with it.

Some of the top-performing and most prestigious State-run schools in Sri Lanka include Royal College, Visakha Vidyalaya, Ananda College, and Devi Balika Vidyalaya in the Colombo District. Trinity College, Girls’ High School, and Mahamaya Girls’ College are among the leading schools in the Kandy District, while Richmond College is one of the most prominent schools in the Galle District.

Generally, these high-performing and prestigious State schools do not face many major issues, as they function efficiently with the support of all stakeholders, particularly their Old Girls’ Associations (OGAs) and Old Boys’ Associations (OBAs). These institutions operate within well-established frameworks of rules, regulations, and traditions, which contribute to their smooth functioning. Discipline in these schools is also maintained at a satisfactory level. This is one of the main reasons for the high demand for admission to these institutions.

However, our focus here is on the remaining National Schools among the 373 in the country, as well as the 9,782 Provincial Schools. In many of these schools, discipline is far from satisfactory, and various types of misconduct and offences are reported from time to time.

Another concern is the frequent collection of money from parents for various purposes, sometimes allegedly without the knowledge of the school principal. Schools often request parents to visit the premises for meetings, activities, and other events. This can place a considerable burden on parents, particularly those employed in the private sector. Such practices appear to be common in many schools across the country. Repeated requests for parents to participate in activities such as shramadana campaigns and other school events can become unreasonable when they occur frequently rather than only a few times a year. Private-sector employees are entitled to limited annual leave, and repeated school-related obligations can create significant difficulties for them.

Another major issue is the tendency in some schools to prioritise the appearance of the school premises over the safety and well-being of students. Many schools have ponds and other structures where rainwater accumulates, creating stagnant water that can serve as breeding grounds for dengue-carrying mosquitoes.

Despite widespread awareness campaigns on dengue prevention, it appears that some school authorities, OGAs, and OBAs do not pay sufficient attention to this issue. In certain instances, there is even strong insistence on maintaining water-retaining features within school premises for aesthetic reasons. Parents, OGAs, and OBAs rarely inspect schools to ensure that such areas are properly maintained and regularly cleaned to prevent mosquito breeding. As a result, schoolchildren may be exposed to unnecessary health risks, including dengue fever.

The relationship between schools and the wider community has, in some instances, become closer than necessary. Individuals from outside the school community are frequently granted access to school premises to participate in activities such as dansals, pirith chanting ceremonies, bana sermons, exhibitions, entertainment programmes, and sporting events.

Some events, particularly pirith chanting ceremonies and bana programmes, are occasionally conducted at night rather than during the daytime or early evening. At times, schoolchildren attend such events without wearing their school uniforms and without being accompanied by their parents. Despite this, schools rarely provide comprehensive safety plans or take adequate measures to safeguard students from potential risks posed by outsiders.

Another concern is that some schools invite individuals who lack the necessary qualifications or professional expertise to conduct lectures and awareness programmes for students. This is particularly evident in certain drug prevention programmes. In some cases, the manner in which these presentations are delivered may inadvertently stimulate curiosity about illicit drugs rather than discourage their use. Instead of highlighting the dangers associated with drug abuse, such programmes may have the opposite effect due to poor presentation methods and a lack of professional competence. There have also been instances where individuals attending school programmes have attempted to promote or sell non-essential products to students.

Educational tours constitute another area of concern. One of the key issues is the absence of a comprehensive and nationally recognised Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) or protocol governing the organisation of school excursions and educational trips.

The tragedy reported from Kirinda during a recent school excursion serves as a stark reminder of the importance of proper planning and risk management. A major concern is that school principals are often required to make critical decisions without a uniform set of guidelines or sufficiently detailed circulars to assist them. This can result in inconsistencies in decision-making from one school to another.

Such disparities could be minimised through the introduction of a comprehensive national framework that clearly outlines procedures, responsibilities, safety requirements, and accountability measures for all school trips and excursions. A standardised approach would help ensure the safety of students while providing school administrators with clear guidance when making important decisions.

Discipline in these schools is also maintained at a satisfactory level. This is one of the main reasons for the high demand for admission to these institutions.

However, our focus here is on the remaining National Schools among the 373 in the country, as well as the 9,782 Provincial Schools. In many of these schools, discipline is far from satisfactory, and various types of misconduct and offences are reported from time to time.

Another concern is the frequent collection of money from parents for various purposes, sometimes allegedly without the knowledge of the school principal. Schools often request parents to visit the premises for meetings, activities, and other events. This can place a considerable burden on parents, particularly those employed in the private sector. Such practices appear to be common in many schools across the country. Repeated requests for parents to participate in activities such as shramadana campaigns and other school events can become unreasonable when they occur frequently rather than only a few times a year. Private-sector employees are entitled to limited annual leave, and repeated school-related obligations can create significant difficulties for them.

Another major issue is the tendency in some schools to prioritise the appearance of the school premises over the safety and well-being of students. Many schools have ponds and other structures where rainwater accumulates, creating stagnant water that can serve as breeding grounds for dengue-carrying mosquitoes.

Despite widespread awareness campaigns on dengue prevention, it appears that some school authorities, OGAs, and OBAs do not pay sufficient attention to this issue. In certain instances, there is even strong insistence on maintaining water-retaining features within school premises for aesthetic reasons. Parents, OGAs, and OBAs rarely inspect schools to ensure that such areas are properly maintained and regularly cleaned to prevent mosquito breeding. As a result, schoolchildren may be exposed to unnecessary health risks, including dengue fever.

The relationship between schools and the wider community has, in some instances, become closer than necessary. Individuals from outside the school community are frequently granted access to school premises to participate in activities such as dansals, pirith chanting ceremonies, bana sermons, exhibitions, entertainment programmes, and sporting events.

Some events, particularly pirith chanting ceremonies and bana programmes, are occasionally conducted at night rather than during the daytime or early evening. At times, schoolchildren attend such events without wearing their school uniforms and without being accompanied by their parents. Despite this, schools rarely provide comprehensive safety plans or take adequate measures to safeguard students from potential risks posed by outsiders.

Another concern is that some schools invite individuals who lack the necessary qualifications or professional expertise to conduct lectures and awareness programmes for students. This is particularly evident in certain drug prevention programmes. In some cases, the manner in which these presentations are delivered may inadvertently stimulate curiosity about illicit drugs rather than discourage their use. Instead of highlighting the dangers associated with drug abuse, such programmes may have the opposite effect due to poor presentation methods and a lack of professional competence. There have also been instances where individuals attending school programmes have attempted to promote or sell non-essential products to students.

Educational tours constitute another area of concern. One of the key issues is the absence of a comprehensive and nationally recognised Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) or protocol governing the organisation of school excursions and educational trips.

The tragedy reported from Kirinda during a recent school excursion serves as a stark reminder of the importance of proper planning and risk management. A major concern is that school principals are often required to make critical decisions without a uniform set of guidelines or sufficiently detailed circulars to assist them. This can result in inconsistencies in decision-making from one school to another.

Such disparities could be minimised through the introduction of a comprehensive national framework that clearly outlines procedures, responsibilities, safety requirements, and accountability measures for all school trips and excursions. A standardised approach would help ensure the safety of students while providing school administrators with clear guidance when making important decisions.

title: No white elephants required - DailyNews
summary:
Holding elections regularly is good, and it is the main indicator of the existence of democracy. But what if holding one specific extra and
non-essential election goes against the wishes of ordinary people and wastes taxpayers’ hard-earned money? No citizen in any country in the world demands such an election, and people never consider it a practice of democracy. This is because democracy should not cause further economic hardships for people. The ordinary people of this country firmly believe that the country is functioning extremely well without Provincial Councils. We are talking about holding the Provincial Council Election.

Holding the Provincial Council Election is not demanded by ordinary Sri Lankan people at this moment. However, the Opposition demands a Provincial Council Election. People do not demand any election at this moment, and they are not interested in Provincial Councils at all. A couple of years ago, the ‘service’ rendered by the nine Provincial Councils was revealed through the National Audit Office Report. The report explains it all.

According to media reports published a couple of years ago, the Provincial Councils had spent Rs. 298 billion on the salaries of employees in 2022, while only Rs. 16 billion was spent on services carried out by them in 2022. The total amount spent on development activities was just four (4) percent of the expenditure. The percentage spent on salaries and other recurrent expenditure was 99 percent. This is the reality, no matter who demands a Provincial Council Election or for what purpose. It is not surprising that no politician from any political party pays attention to this issue because they and their henchmen get paid for doing nothing in Provincial Councils. The other set of culprits are the lazy public servants attached to all nine (9) Provincial Councils. Provincial Councils are just a waste of public money.

This situation tells the entire story. There should be an end to this waste of public funds. This practice, which continued for decades, is one major reason for the grave financial crisis the country faced in 2022.

The entire country can clearly see that the demand of all opposition political parties is not based on the people’s welfare. What they all want are salaries for their henchmen and nothing else, regardless of what happens to the country’s economy. The selfishness of politicians belonging to all political parties is clearly indicated here. By now, Sri Lankan people have understood the real nature of local politicians, who are only worried about themselves and their loved ones. Sri Lankan people stand here today as poor ordinary citizens because of the selfishness and greed that existed over the past several decades. They did not even plan development projects properly at the rural level in the past.

It is very interesting to examine how Provincial Councils and Pradeshiya Sabhas ‘served’ the Sri Lankan people during the past several decades. The functioning of Provincial Councils, Municipal Councils, Urban Councils, Pradeshiya Sabhas, etc. was extremely pathetic. They never gave approval for anything without obtaining bribes from ordinary people. This is what ordinary people experienced in their day-to-day lives during the past several decades. Those Provincial Councils and all the other bodies never delivered any service worthy of the tax money paid by ordinary people. They do not even remove garbage properly or on time. So, what is the point of talking about their ‘maintenance’, ‘projects’ and ‘programmes’?

According to the existing law, all houses located within 100 metres of main roads should pay tax to the Pradeshiya Sabhas, but those Pradeshiya Sabhas never collect garbage from homes that pay tax but are located within 100 metres of the main road. They only collect garbage from houses located beside main roads. There is no point in talking about other services. This situation exists especially in Pradeshiya Sabhas. It is people who get together and provide services to the public, not the Pradeshiya Sabhas.

Those bodies started new tactics a decade or two ago to snatch people’s hard-earned money. Even for a small matter, they provide people with a set of documents and charge money for handling them. What they can do is enter data online while the customer is sitting in front of them at the office. Usually, the officials of Pradeshiya Sabhas visit sites (homes, land, etc.) with their drivers. The bribe is usually taken by the driver or another person and not by the official directly. From the peon to the Pradeshiya Sabha Chairman, all take bribes for everything. Technical Officers (public servants) are the worst. This is what ordinary Sri Lankan people experienced during the past several decades when obtaining any type of service from any Pradeshiya Sabha or Provincial Council in the country. The people brought the National People’s Power (NPP) Government into power with the objective of getting rid of that long-lasting corruption network.

Whenever poor or helpless people approach a Pradeshiya Sabha or a Provincial Council to obtain any service, those institutions waste the valuable time and money of such people as much as possible and make them visit the office more than 100 times for one purpose. Even after visiting 100 times, those employees never do their job. By now, almost all Sri Lankan citizens are fed up with Pradeshiya Sabhas and Provincial Councils because those state institutions never help them and only harass them whenever they visit to obtain a service.

When powerful or rich individuals approach them, they happily deliver the service as soon as possible, perhaps within hours or days, because of the bribe money they receive or due to fear. They see various defects in house plans brought by poor and helpless people but never see any defect in building plans brought by the rich and powerful.

Often, those poor families never get the chance to build their own houses before their deaths because of the cussedness of employees attached to those state bodies and the other bodies coming under their purview. By the time they receive approval for their house plans, the aged parents are dead or the family has already spent all the money they had collected and kept to build the house.

Enough is enough. These types of ill practices that have existed in some state bodies for several decades need to be changed as soon as possible, especially before holding any election and appointing new members to them. Elections appoint members, but not public servants who have been serving in those State institutions for decades until retirement. They are the real curse.

The best thing that can be done is to get rid of the Provincial Council (sick) system, which did not exist in Sri Lanka before 1987. Sri Lanka’s Provincial Councils were established by the 13th Amendment to the Constitution in 1987, with the first eight councils implemented in February 1988. This system devolved power to a secondary legislative level for regional administration. But the ordinary people of Sri Lanka did not demand it and, by now, hate it more than any other state body because of the ‘treatment’ they have received from it during the past 38 years.

If Provincial Council Elections need to be held for some reason, the individuals who contest from various political parties should be decided by the people and not by the political leadership of those parties. This is the only way to stop crooks from receiving nominations and becoming candidates at the election through various political parties. It is the right of the people to decide who represents them in Provincial Councils, and political leaders have nothing to do with selecting them. The people of Sri Lanka should not vote for candidates nominated by political party leaders. People should be given the right to nominate their own representatives. How can political party leaders offer crooks nominations, making them representatives of the people? This ill practice, which has taken place during the past 38 years (almost four decades), cannot be accepted and should be eliminated starting this year. It is the people who should hand over the list of their representatives to political party leaders for nomination at the next Provincial Council Election. There is no legal amendment required to do this because it has nothing to do with election law. This process comes before nomination lists are prepared.

title: Dangerous impact of child sexual abuse - DailyNews
summary:
Children are the most vulnerable members of our society and can be victims of various forms of violence. Child sexual abuse is an
umbrella term used to describe a wide range of sexual activities that take place between a child and an adult, in which the child does not fully comprehend and is unable to give consent. Child sexual abuse is a public health issue that has been associated with a variety of negative social outcomes.

Numerous terms have been used to illustrate child sexual abuse including -child sexual assault, child sexual victimisation and child exploitation.The term ‘children’ in this article refers to individuals under 18 years of age.Almost 90% of sexually abused children are abused by someone they know.Understanding more about child sexual abuse- including who might perpetrate it, helps us to prevent and better respond to it.Sadly society often treats victims of abuse with doubt, which makes abusers feel more confident that they will get away with their crime.

Victim-survivors of child sexual abuse can be affected in a wide range of ways, but the nature and extent of the impacts experienced vary: no two individuals are affected in the same way.Sexual abuse can affect children’s psychosocial development and attachment, with impacts on sexual functioning as well as relationships in both adolescence and adulthood.Childhood sexual abuse is proven to have short and long-term negative consequences to the innocent victim. Physical consequences of such abuse include injuries, unintended pregnancy and genital infections. Those who were sexually abused in childhood are more inclined to develop behavioural and psychological problems such as sleep disturbance, social-related difficulties, eating disorders, self-esteem issues, fear, anxiety and depression.

When most people imagine a child molester, they envision an ugly man coaxing children, with chocolates.The vast majority of child molesters are adults who seduce children through subtle intimidation and persuasion. The criminal abuseris known to the child or the parents. These dirty predators betray the respect and trust placed on them by the innocent children and their parents. The abusers are mentally abnormal individuals.It’s important to note that deviant behavior – whether due to psychological disorders (e.g., pedophilia), hedonistic impulsivity or antisocial traits – tend to persist across the lifespan.Forensic psychologists are frequently requested to assess and treat individuals who have been charged or convicted of sexual offences against child victims.Certain personality traits may also contribute to an individual’s likelihood of engaging in abuse. These can include low self-esteem, narcissism, a lack of empathy and more.

Criminal child molesters come from all walks of life. They can be male or female, rich or poor, employed or unemployed, religious or non-religious, from any ethnicity. In cases where the child molester is not known by the victim, he or she may use a variety of methods to gain access including force, fear or acts of bribery. The savage abuser may pretend to be friendly, kind, caring, pious and trustworthy.The intra-familial molester is usually an adult male (father, stepfather, grandfather or live-in boyfriend of the mother).The molestation usually occurs over an extended period of time, occasionally into the victim’s adulthood. Through intimidation, the child is made to feel responsible for the molestation and for keeping the acts secret. This secret is normally kept between the offender and the victim or within the immediate family.

One common misperception is that all child sexual abuse perpetrators are paedophiles. The terms ‘paedophile’ and ‘child sexual abuse perpetrator’ are often used interchangeably. However, the terms have different meanings. Paedophiles (as defined by the Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders) are individuals who are preferentially or solely sexually attracted to prepubescent children, generally 13 years or less.Fixed, persistent perpetrators tend to have a long-term sexual attraction to children or young people.Studies of child sexual abuse show that men are more likely than women to commit sexual abuse in different environments (such as institutional, online or in the family home).

Sexual enjoyment can be a motive for abusing a child but it usually combines with other motives.Related motives that criminal predators might have, to abuse a child include wanting to:control someone and feel powerful, act out difficult emotions or fantasies andwillingly hurt someone for pleasure. Most child abusers are not only sexually interested in children. Children are often targeted for sexual abuse because they are usually vulnerable than adults. This makes the child abuser a coward. Abusive people find it easier to act on their desires if they have convinced themselves that what they want to do is ok.They may tell themselves that: they are more important than the children they abuse the abuse isn’t harmful and they deserve or are entitled to it.Some child abusers may have psychological issues that are contributing such as- problems controlling their emotions, an obsession with sex (hidden under a mask of being a good person) and difficulty feeling for other people or understanding social rules.

Protecting children is one of the most important things the police do. It is important to remember that child abuse is a serious crime and law enforcement has a legal duty and responsibility to respond swiftly without fear or favour. Globally police officers investigate suspected crimes involving children and arrest perpetrators. They play a significant role in monitoring sex offenders. They can take a child in danger to a place of safety, and they can seek restrictions on offenders’ contact with children. They also play an important role, working with other organizations, in ensuring children’s protection and well-being.

Failure to respond properly to child abuse cases from the outset (e.g., failure of the responding police officer to obtain and verify information, make proper police entries with all available evidence) can result in cases being dismissed in court. Across the world, any guilty child abuser must not walk away freely. Investigating officers must never discount children’s statements about who is abusing them, where and how the abuse is occurring, or what types of acts occurred.Responding police must treat the scene as a crime scene (even if abuse has occurred in the past) and not as the site of a social problem.

The role of law enforcement in child abuse cases is to investigate to determine if a violation of criminal law occurred, identify and apprehend the offender, and file appropriate criminal charges. The response of law enforcement to child abuse needs to be consistent.Crimes of abuse are not usually isolated incidents; they take place over a period of time, with increasing severity. Sadly in most child sexual abuse cases, there is no conclusive medical evidence that sexual abuse occurred. Moreover, it occurs in a private place with no witnesses to the sexual abuse.Social workers, doctors, judges and police officers all have important roles to play. All must work together with a common concern- the welfare and safety of the child victim.The community has a legal, moral and ethical responsibility to assume an active role in responding to sexual abuseof innocent children. Globally increasing awareness among national and community stakeholders about child abuse and child protection creates safer environments.

title: Next generation steps in - DailyNews
summary:
I too was a guy who wanted to change the world. But I thought I could do it alone! Did one man win the Trojan War? Achilles was the greatest
warrior of the Trojan War. But did he single handedly win the Trojan War? NO. The Trojan War was won by an army. The Greeks won the Trojan War. The world is always changing, but do you want to be that change? What about those heroes of old? Those mighty men? Those warriors? Heracles, who performed his twelve labors, battling terrifying monsters like the Hydra, that monstrous serpent, and journeying to the underworld and facing Cerberus, the fearsome, multi-headed dog. Or what about Theseus, who slayed the Minotaur? What about Perseus who beheaded Medusa and turned a sea monster to stone by showing it the head of the Medusa? They were not intimidated by what they had to do. They rose to the challenge.

In life do you want to be a benchwarmer or do you want to go out there and fight for what you believe in? Many people have told young guys and girls that they cannot change the world. They were wrong. You can change the world. BUT you cannot do it alone. That is where so many youth get it wrong. You can change the world, but you cannot do it alone. You need to focus on the “WE” and not the “I”.

Today so many youth have fallen through the cracks. Lost sheep I call them. So, I say let’s do this for them! Let’s win this for them! Let’s change the world for them!Today the youth need to be given a voice and a seat at the table. In order to create a stronger country, the youth need to be given a voice. Let’s create heroes.

Today’s youth will decide the fate of millions and billions in the future. They will decide the final outcome. The world is filled with homeless people and people living in extreme poverty. The youth can change all of that and bring prosperity. The youth can put an end to War and violence. The youth can work together and heal those with medical conditions. So many have struggled for change in history. Is their sacrifice in vain? So don’t hang your head in defeat. You are the youth. You can create change!Together you stand!

Designed as a platform for meaningful engagement and action, the initiative seeks to ensure that the voices of Millennials and Gen Z are placed at the center of national transformation.

GLOBAL UNITES officially launched a nationwide youth led policy initiative aimed at advancing national unity, justice, social cohesion and youth development in Sri Lanka.At the press conference,GLOBAL UNITES introduced a series of proposed policy recommendations developed through extensive consultation, research and youth engagement efforts focused on building a more inclusive, peaceful and equitable future for all Sri Lankans.

THE RECOMMENDATIONS ARE CENTERED AROUND 3 KEY NATIONAL PRIORITIES

*The first is Youth Development and Advancement. It calls for a comprehensive long -term strategy to address the structural challenges facing young people while expanding access to education, employment, entrepreneurship and global opportunities. It also aims to equip youth to become innovative, resilient and globally connected citizens, while fostering leadership, civic participation and social mobility across communities.

*The second focus area is National Unity, Justice and Social Cohesion. These recommendations emphasize building an inclusive and shared Sri Lankan identity, strengthening trust across ethnic, religious and regional communities and promoting democratic participation, justice and social healing to create a peaceful and thriving society for future generations.

*The third area addresses Grievances and Structural Inequalities through a transformative framework that seeks to respond meaningfully to historic and present -day grievances, inequality, exclusion and marginalisation. The goal is to promote restorative justice, equitable development, and a stronger sense of dignity belonging and opportunity for all communities.

Additional initiatives unveiled include “Platform Next Gen”, a national oratory competition designed to amplify youth voices, and the “Mage Rata” interview series, which will feature diverse Sri Lankan perspectives on national transformation.  Opportunities for volunteers and partners to support outreach, media, research and youth engagement efforts were also introduced.

President and Founder of Global Unites, Prashan De Visser,explained that Global Unites is all about creating and promoting unity amongst Sri Lankans from diverse backgrounds, because when you taken Sri Lankan history there seems to be a recurring pattern of unrest. Here the youth are directly affected.

“Here we need to be proactive and vigilant and we must constantly strive to champion unity with our collective strength. Here, we need to be even more determined to create togetherness. This must be done through the youth. Here we need to guard against divisions and groups who try and create division. They are a great danger. Here there needs to be foresight. We must prevent problems from occurring. We need to do this for the generations to come. Here we need to give the youth a voice and we need to listen to what they have to say, because the youth have a lot to say. We invite the youth to come forward,” pointed out De Visser.

He added that we have to address the problems of the youth, because there will be various factors that will try and take advantage of the dissatisfaction of the youth to promote their agenda. There must be a focus on Justice and harmony. There is much to learn here. There must be a national policy here as well. Here our Sri Lankan identity and unity must be celebrated. Let us not repeat our mistakes,but learn from the past, and learn from each other says De Visser.

Global Unites Member, Chaminda Jayasekara, added that Global Unites always tries to promote a Sri Lanka with an “inclusive identity”. This means a united Sri Lanka. “We are doing all of this for our youth. Even though the civil war is over, our country still bears those scars and hurts. It has left deep marks on Sri Lankan society. I feel the tensions still persist, and I feel that a united Sri Lankan identity, harmony and sustainable peace has not reached the ground level yet. Here the youth can play an important role in bringing change,” said Jayasekara.

Here there needs to be a dialogue. There needs to be discussion. There needs to be an exchange of ideas amongst the youth at the grassroot level. .e.g.“how do we build this country?”Jayasekara here pointed out that education is a necessity. It is important for the youth to understand what they need to do in order to bring about real social change and stop the repetition of mistakes. They need to understand what their responsibilities are. They need to understand what issues are relevant to them. “We need to connect youth at the ground level/ the grassroot level. We are reaching out to political leaders,and we need to make an impact here. We need to create discourse at the grassroot level. We need to know the ideas of the youth. We need to give them that opportunity.”

Global Unites Member, Indunil Bandarapointed out that the economic wellbeing is so important for the youth. When the economy suffers, the individual suffers and we know this very well through experience. When the economy suffers various problems emerge.When there is conflict in society, the economy suffers. This is why a Sri Lanka united is the best outcome that we all desire. “The youth understand all of this and they are intelligent. The youth have potential. They have fresh perspective and new ideas. They must be given a voice.”

Here, if the youth is given a voice, the probability of Sri Lanka falling into an unruly state will lessen. Let the youth and adults combine forces. Here vision and research has come together, to deliver excellent results.

It has been 20 years of engaging youth. Global Unites Member, Urshella Hissam, spoke about the NATIONAL SURVEY they are conducting in 25 districts in Sri Lanka, 2500 young people. They want to hear the opinions of Gen Z and Millennials. They want to make sure that this generation does not make the same mistakes. The goal is to try and understand their mindset through the survey. They are doing consultations in all 9 provinces. What are these youth concerns? We need to guard against groups that create divisions in Sri Lanka through promoting fear and violence.

“We have a three -pronged approach, and we are keen on hearing from you. We are collecting ideas. Our aim is to collect at least 2500 voices of yours. So, this is your chance to share your views on reconciliation, justice and national unity. We want to develop a comprehensive policy at the end of this journey. We will also hear your ideas through these consultations.”

THE FINAL POLICY PROPOSAL

The final policy proposal is expected to be formally presented to National leaders including the President, Prime Minister, Minister of Justice, Minister of Youth Affairs, Leader of the Opposition and leaders of major political parties. The proposal will also be shared with the United Nations and international partners supporting reconciliation, justice and youth development efforts in Sri Lanka.

title: Organizing Dansel during the vesak festival - DailyNews
summary:
People who visit Dansel scattered islandwide need to be vigilant about food safety and all related issues in order to prevent food poisoning. It is the sole responsibility of people to refrain from eating food from any Dansel that do not follow the relevant health guidelines.

The Vesak Festival was held on May 30 and 31. Offering Dansel commenced with the Vesak Festival, and it will continue over the next
few weeks all over the country. Offering Dansel is one of the main traditions in Sri Lanka. Therefore, it is important to ensure public health safety while offering and visiting Dansel.

This year, health authorities have made a special request to the public to offer hot drinks such as tea and coffee instead of refrigerated soft drinks, considering the current health situation in the country.

Offering Dansel should be done according to the guidelines issued by the health authorities, and they are available on the Epidemiology Unit website: http://www.epid.gov.lk/

People who visit Dansel scattered islandwide need to be vigilant about food safety and all related issues in order to prevent food poisoning. It is the sole responsibility of people to refrain from eating food from any Dansel that do not follow the relevant health guidelines.

In order to do this, people need to be vigilant about specific things such as the appearance of food handlers (whether they are wearing gloves, head covers, face masks, etc., and whether they look healthy without any visible illnesses), the appearance and warmth of food, whether there are flies on uncovered food, where the drinking water comes from, how food is being served, etc.

Registration of all Dansel with the nearest MOH is mandatory. The Public Health Inspectors’ Union said registration of Dansel is a must. The organizers are required to inform the PHI of their respective area and provide details of the location and nature of the event. Dansel should not be organised close to toilets and drains.

The day before a Dansel is held, PHIs will inspect whether the location is suitable, including waste disposal, water quality, and cooking conditions, to ensure operations align with the Food Hygiene Regulations of 2011. Therefore, all organizers of Dansel should meet the relevant requirements by the time of the PHIs’ visit.

Inspectors will pay special attention to certain things during their inspection. PHIs will conduct checks both before and after the events to verify sanitary conditions and proper environmental management. Legal action will be taken against those conducting unregistered or unhygienic Dansel.

Waste management is another key part of organizing any Dansel. Organizers must implement a structured waste disposal plan from start to finish. This is a must. All garbage bins should be properly covered with lids.

Water safety is a must for Dansel. The use of water from the National Water Supply and Drainage Board remains the priority; otherwise, water must come from verified safe sources. Clean, safe, fresh, and hot (highly recommended) drinking water should be made available for all visitors to Dansel. All utensils used need to be thoroughly cleaned with water and soap.

Hygiene facilities are another essential part of organizing Dansel. Food handlers and those involved in preparation and serving will also be subject to checks to ensure public safety. They should wear head covers, face masks, and gloves. They should not suffer from any communicable disease or skin disease. Hand-washing stations and sanitizers must be available for all visitors. All food and drinks should be protected from flies.

Food freshness is a must at all Dansel. Organizers were advised to use only safe and hygienic ingredients when preparing food for distribution. The time elapsed between preparing food and serving it should not exceed four (4) hours. Do not use old newspapers for food packaging, as printing ink can be toxic and contaminate the food.

It is not acceptable for anyone to chew betel, consume alcohol, visit Dansel after consuming alcohol, or smoke in and around Dansel premises.

title: Paid in   generosity - DailyNews
summary:
We can perhaps call the roadside dansela as one of a kind social institution produced by the Sri Lankan edition of Buddhist civilization. What appears to be a temporary food stall erected for a religious festival is, in reality, the living epitome of an idea that stretches across millennia.

The story, if it exists at all, begins long before the birth of Prince Siddhartha.

The line of vehicles slows down to a halt. A young man in a white T-shirt walks into the traffic. He carries a flag. Motorcyclists pull over.
A bus conductor leans out of a window. Families and families pour out of tuk-tuks. And those travelling in BYDs, the cars that invite their owners to ‘Build Your Dreams’, join motorists of every make and model in answering a different call. It is not the pursuit of some personal dream, but cherishing a moment of generosity.

Because of what is going on nearby. Beneath a temporary canopy stitched together from bamboo poles and cloth, volunteers are ladling rice onto plates while children pass cups of tea down a human chain. No one asks where they come from. No one asks what ethnic group they belong to, what language they speak, how much money they earn, or which political party they support.

Such divisions vanish into thin air. The corporate executive, the labourer, the student and the pilgrim alike stand in the same queue to be handed the same meal and sit side by side beneath the same illuminated lanterns.

We can perhaps call the roadside dansela as one of a kind social institution produced by the Sri Lankan edition of Buddhist civilization. What appears to be a temporary food stall erected for a religious festival is, in reality, the living epitome of an idea that stretches across millennia.

The story, if it exists at all, begins long before the birth of Prince Siddhartha.

Generosity shares common grounds across the world’s great religions. Christianity elevates charity among its highest virtues. Islam institutionalises giving through zakat. Hindu traditions consider dana as a duty that loosens attachment to worldly possessions. The act of giving is there wherever human beings exists.

Generosity stands at the head of the ten perfections (dasa paramita). The perfections are the qualities cultivated by a Bodhisatta over countless ages in preparation for Buddhahood. Before wisdom, before meditation, before enlightenment itself – and before the rest of the paramitas – comes the willingness to give.

According to the Buddhavamsa, the future Gautama Buddha was once an ascetic named Sumedha living during the age of Dipankara Buddha. One day, as crowds gathered in anticipation of Dipankara’s arrival, Sumedha encountered a stretch of muddy ground along the path the Buddha would soon travel. He spread his own body over the mud in order to offer himself as a bridge so that the Buddha and his disciples could pass uninterrupted.

Dipankara Buddha perceived the ascetic’s potential and pronounced a prophecy. In a future age Sumedha would himself become a Buddha. That prophecy transformed a single act of giving into a spiritual programme spanning the ages. Buddhist literature describes this evolution in increasingly demanding stages: the giving of possessions, the giving of one’s own body and, ultimately, the willingness to sacrifice life itself for the welfare of others.

The central question was never what one possessed. The question was what one was prepared to let go.

If we choose this lens to widen our scope, the modern dansela becomes something far deeper than average seasonal hospitality. Each free meal, each cup of tea, each volunteer standing by a roadside represents that ancient principle.

The Buddha’s teachings are remembered for the penetrating analysis of suffering, impermanence and the restless nature of the human mind. Less frequently discussed is their equally sophisticated understanding of greed.

Long before economists debated wealth accumulation and consumer culture, Buddhist storytellers were exploring a question that remains modern: why do human beings cling to things?

Remember Illisa Jataka? Illisa was wealthy beyond measure. He possessed land, riches and influence. Yet his abundance brought him no happiness. He was stingy. He refused to share with neighbours, withheld generosity from servants and denied himself even modest comforts.

Excerpted below is Robert Chalmers’ translation of the Illisa Jataka.

“The Elder [Arahant Moggallana] began to pace to and fro in his place in the air! “What will you get by pacing to and fro?” said the Treasurer [Illisa]! “You may sit cross-legged in meditation in the air,—but still you’ll get nothing.” The Elder sat down with legs crossed! Then said the Treasurer, “What will you get by sitting there? You may come and stand on the window-sill; but even that won’t get you any-thing!” The Elder took his stand on the window-sill. “What will you get by standing on the window-sill? Why, you may belch smoke, and yet you’ll still get nothing!” said the Treasurer. Then the Elder belched forth smoke till the whole palace was filled with it. The Treasurer’s eyes began to smart as though pricked with needles; and, for fear at last that his house might be set on fire, he checked himself from adding—“You won’t get anything even if you burst into flames.” Thought he to himself, “This Elder is most persistent! He simply won’t go away empty-handed! I must have just one cake given him.” So he said to his wife, “My dear, cook one little cake and give it to the sage to get rid of him.”

So she mixed quite a little dough in a crock. But the dough swelled and swelled till it filled the whole crock, and grew to be a great big cake! “What a lot you must have used!” exclaimed the Treasurer at the sight. And he himself with the tip of a spoon took a very little of the dough, and put that in the oven to bake. But that tiny piece of dough grew larger than the first lump; and, one after another, every piece of dough he took became ever so big! Then he lost heart and said to his wife, “You give him a cake, dear.” But, as soon as she took one cake from the basket, at once all the other cakes stuck fast to it. So she cried out to her husband that all the cakes had stuck together, and that she could not part them.

“Oh, I’ll soon part them,” said he,—but found he could not!”

Psychological Transformation

The transformation is not economic. It is psychological.

The cultural genius of the dansela lies precisely in this transformation. What begins as personal generosity becomes collective generosity. What begins as an individual virtue becomes a social experience.

This ancient narrative illuminates a central feature of the dansela tradition. A dansela is not designed as a private act of charity performed discreetly between donor and recipient. It is intentionally public.

When Buddhism took root during the reign of King Devanampiyatissa, generosity ceased to be solely a personal religious practice. It gradually became embedded within the structure of governance.

The chronicles describe an era in which kings sought not merely to rule but to embody Buddhist ethical principles. Giving was elevated into a matter of public responsibility. The concept of dana became intertwined with ideas of righteous kingship, social welfare and civic duty.

The Mahapali Hall is believed to have been built by King Devanampiyatissa in the 3rd century BC and had been expanded and supported by many other sovereigns. Situated near monasteries, urban centres and important routes of travel, they served as places where food, shelter and assistance could be provided to those in need. Their purpose extended beyond religious merit. They functioned as an early welfare infrastructure and offered support to pilgrims, monks, travellers and the vulnerable.

Archaeological remains in the ancient capital of Anuradhapura still bear witness to the scale of this undertaking. Among the most striking relics is the massive stone rice trough known as the Bath Oruwa.

Long before modern highways crisscrossed Sri Lanka, the island’s most important journeys were made on foot. Pilgrims travelled through forests, crossed rivers, climbed mountains and followed narrow paths worn smooth by generations of travellers. The journey to Sri Pada, known to many outside Sri Lanka as Adam’s Peak, was among the most demanding. Weeks could pass before a pilgrim reached the summit. Along the way there were wild animals, unpredictable weather and the simple exhaustion of traversing difficult terrain.

Yet these hardships also gave rise to one of the island’s most enduring traditions of hospitality.

The mountain occupied a unique place in the religious imagination of South Asia. Buddhists revered it as the site bearing the sacred footprint of the Buddha. Hindus associated it with Lord Shiva. Christians and Muslims developed their own sacred narratives around the peak. For centuries, pilgrims of different faiths converged upon the same mountain, often sharing the same routes, shelters and resting places.

Villagers established ambalamas, simple wayside rest houses where weary travellers could pause. Food and water were offered freely. Temporary danselas appeared during pilgrimage seasons. A traveller’s religion mattered less than the fact that he or she was tired, hungry and far from home.

The practical necessity of survival gradually became an ethical habit. Generosity turned into a language spoken across religious boundaries.

This explains why the dansela could speak for inclusivity even today. Its roots may reach to the depth of Buddhist philosophy, but its social expression transcends any sectarian identity. One does not need to profess a particular belief to receive a meal at a Vesak dansela. The act of giving is directed toward humanity before affiliation.

For a brief moment on the roadside, the world seems to agree with that. Then the traffic begins to move again.
